title: Extraordinary thermophysical properties of an aluminum-matrix composite processed by gas pressure infiltration
abstract: Abstract Several components used in space applications can benefit from cooling systems made from materials combining high thermal conductivities with low densities. Additionally, a low coefficient of thermal expansion is desirable to reduce mechanical stresses under geometrically constrained conditions. In the present work, this property portfolio is investigated with a material system of aluminum-matrix composites using pitch-based carbon fibers. These MMC materials are realized using gas pressure infiltration technology. Different layup configurations allow for tailoring the directionality of the heat transfer. The thermophysical properties show extraordinarily high values for the unidirectional scenarios and good properties for the bidirectional and the quasi-isotropic layups. Finally, a set of samples is studied in a thermal shock scenario, which evidences the formation of weak cracks with, however, very modest effects on the thermal conductivity values.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Several applications used in space components require high thermal conductivity combined with low thermal expansion. Thermal sinks for high performance electronics are among these [ 1 ], entailing the removal of heat through highly conductive materials and low thermal expansion to avoid the disintegration because of different thermally induced strains and the resultant strain incompatibilities [ 2 ,  3 ]. Another critical aspect of the addressed application is the material response to thermal shocks – conditions, which are commonly observed in diverse space applications [ 4 ].

Metal-matrix composites (MMCs) combine the properties of different materials in most instances metals and ceramics. These material combinations unlock a diverse tailor-ability of the material characteristics [ 2 ]. Depending on the application, these materials are tuned toward abrasion resistance, hardness, electrical conductivity or thermal conductivity [ 5 ,  6 ]. The present work focuses on the use of fiber-reinforced aluminum MMCs to tailor the thermal conductivity in combination with a low density enabling light-weight construction [ 7 ,  8 ]. Fibers based on carbon show good thermal conduction, specifically the pitch-based carbon fibers [ 9 ]. Their introduction into a metal matrix with a high fiber content corresponds to a potential means for realizing high thermal conductivity combined with low density.

The properties of carbon fiber/aluminum (Cf/Al) composites are critically governed by the characteristics of the carbon–aluminum interface. Pronounced interfacial reactions can degrade the carbon reinforcement and promote the formation of brittle interfacial phases, thereby, impairing both thermal and mechanical performance [ 10 ]. Notably, the interfacial reactivity between carbon fibers and the aluminum matrix becomes significant at temperatures exceeding 500 °C [ 11 ], and the reaction kinetics strongly depend on temperature [ 12 ]. Microstructural investigations have consistently identified Al₄C₃ as the principal interfacial reaction product in Cf/Al systems. Both its formation and morphological evolution exert a decisive influence on interfacial bonding strength and, consequently, on the overall performance of the composite [ 13 ].

To mitigate detrimental interfacial reactions, various strategies have been explored. These include surface modification of the carbon fibers as well as compositional tailoring of the aluminum matrix through alloying additions (e.g., Mg, Ti, Si) [ 14 ,  15 ]. Among these approaches, alloying represents a particularly efficient and economically viable method for engineering the interfacial structure and enhancing matrix properties. In particular, the addition of magnesium has been reported to improve both infiltration behavior and mechanical properties [ 15 ].

Beyond material design, processing conditions play a crucial role, as interfacial reactions are diffusion-controlled and therefore strongly dependent on temperature and time. A range of processing routes has been employed for the fabrication of Cf/Al composites, including spark plasma sintering (SPS) [ 16 ], vacuum hot pressing (VHP) [ 17 ], and liquid metal infiltration [ 18 ,  19 ]. While SPS and VHP enable consolidation at comparatively low temperatures, they often result in insufficient interfacial bonding between matrix and reinforcement, which may compromise the thermophysical performance of the composites. Most reported studies focus on (short) pitch-based carbon fibers embedded in Al or Al–Si matrices, typically produced via hot pressing of powder precursors in the solid or semi-solid state at temperatures 600–660 °C for extended durations of 30–100 min [ 16 ,  17 ,  20 ]. In contrast, liquid infiltration techniques inherently involve higher processing temperatures, which may promote interfacial reactions between carbon and aluminum when insufficient process conditions are selected [ 14 ]. For gas pressure infiltration utilizing aluminum and diamond particles, Zhang et al. [ 21 ] reported that strict control of infiltration temperature, pressure and dwell time is essential for the interfacial microstructures and thermal conductivities of composites. For optimized process conditions, a thermal conductivity of up to 760 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ has been measured [ 21 ]. In this context, gas pressure infiltration represents a promising processing route for Cf/Al composites, as it enables rapid infiltration at reduced temperatures and shorter processing times, thereby limiting interfacial reactions while ensuring adequate matrix–fiber bonding.

This work explores the use of gas pressure infiltration (see e.g. [ 22 ,  23 ]). to manufacture MMCs with unidirectional (UD), bidirectional (0/90) and quasi-isotropic (QI) fiber arrangements/layups. This process enables the precise thermal control needed for the important interface between the fibers and the metal matrix [ 2 ]. The structural integrity and microstructure of the samples are analyzed using optical light microscopy (OLM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The thermophysical properties are analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), dilatometry, and laser-flash analysis (LFA). The results demonstrate that the processing route allows to manufacture such MMCs, which then achieve high thermal conductivity values in different directions of the composite (depending on the layup). Good structural integrity of the material is obtained. To assess the condition after a thermal shock, additional samples underwent nitrogen quenching and were subsequently metallographically analyzed as well as potential resulting changes in their thermophysical properties. The presented results showcase the potential applicability of MMCs using pitch-based fibers in aluminum-matrices manufactured by gas pressure infiltration for challenging thermal management applications.

sections.heading: Materials and processing
paragraphs: The samples analyzed in this paper were manufactured using gas pressure infiltration. This technology belongs to the liquid infiltration methods and is carried out using a pressure casting equipment. Pressure and temperature are constantly monitored throughout the infiltration sequence. The equipment used for the present investigation uses one pressure sensor and three thermocouples. Prior to infiltration, a fiber preform and a matrix feeder are manufactured. These components are then assembled in an autoclave. After application of a vacuum environment and sufficient heating, the infiltration process is started. After a short pressurization time, the mold is cooled to ensure rapid solidification and to omit the formation of carbides at the fiber/matrix interface (see Appendix  A ). After the infiltration procedure the MMC material must be extracted from the gas pressure unit and mold.

For the present investigations a pitch-based fiber Dialead K13D2U from Mitsubishi Chemical was used. This fiber has among the highest reported thermal conductivity values with ~ 800 W/mK. The matrix consisted of an AlMg5 alloy with a thermal conductivity of approximately 115 W/mK. Samples were fabricated with unidirectional (UD) fiber orientation (two sets with approximately 60 vol% (variant UD1) and 70 vol% (variant UD2) fiber content), with bidirectional 0° and 90° fiber arrangement orientation and with a quasi-isotropic arrangement containing 0°, ± 45° and 90° oriented fiber layers. For the latter two variants the fiber content was kept constant at approximately 60 vol%.

Thermal shock treatments were conducted on three samples of the UD2 variant and results were analyzed in detail. The heating cycle was done in a Heraeus model 6000 furnace, and for the cooling a titanium bowl was prepared filled with liquid nitrogen. The tests started with the heating phase to 200 °C for a holding period of 15 min and quenching in liquid nitrogen, where the sample was kept for additional 15 min. This sequence was conducted three times. After a 4th heating cycle, the trial ended with cooling to room temperature. The sample was sectioned at several positions resulting in five specimens to receive representative information about the cracks present after the treatment.

sections.heading: Material characterization
paragraphs: For analysis of the microstructure and the thermal shock results, pieces of the samples have been cut, embedded, and prepared by grinding (with SiC paper, end grain 2400) and polishing with a suspension (1 μm) employing a Tegramin-30 machine. Analysis of the fiber arrangement and microstructure was conducted by optical light microscopy (OLM) using an Olympus BX60M microscope. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) investigations were conducted using a Tescan Mira 3 microscope at 20 kV acceleration voltage in back-scattered electron mode.

DSC measurements were conducted with a disc-type heat flow DSC NETZSCH DSC 204 F1. Three samples per material were placed into 85 µl Al crucibles and measured from − 10 °C up to 30 °C to evaluate the actual heat flow at 25 °C and constant heating rate conditions (β = 10 K m -1 ). The experiments were conducted in a constant N 2  flow of 40 ml min -1 . The standard reference material sapphire (α-Al 2 O 3 ) was measured at the same conditions to evaluate the actual specific heat capacity of the investigated samples.

Thermal diffusivity measurements are based on the Laser Flash (LFA) technique and the Cowan Model [ 24 ]. The measurement device is a NETZSCH LFA 427 with a special laminate sample holder system. The samples were milled into 10 mm x 2 mm rods in the respective directions and lined up and clamped together using the graphite laminate sample holder to measure the thermal diffusivity in the desired plane direction. A standard Al 2 O 3  sample holder for cubic samples was used to determine the thermal diffusivity perpendicular to the plane direction of the composite. The applied laser pulse on the bottom side of the sample is generated with Rofin/Baasel Starweld 40 W Nd: YAG-Laser with a pulse width of 0.3 ms and a laser lamp voltage of 700 V. The InSb detector detects the IR response of the upper surface of the sample after the laser pulse was applied. 3000 signal points were recorded per shot while the length of the acquisition was changed according to the actual half time of the signal response. The recorded signal response is then used to evaluate the thermal diffusivity according to the Cowan model. All measurements were conducted at 25 °C measured with a Type K thermocouple close to the sample and were performed under atmospheric conditions, no additional gases were used during the experiments. To validate the measurements an Al 2 O 3 -TiC material was used as reference. This material corresponds to a certified reference material available from the National Metrology Institute of Japan for thermal diffusivity measurements using the LFA method. The thermal conductivity, λ. was then calculated according to: λ = α × ρ × c p , where α refers to the thermal diffusivity, ρ to the material’s density and c p  to the specific heat capacity.

The coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) was measured using a DANTEC DYNAMICS system. The device operates on the principle of digital image correlation (DIC), which tracks changes in the sample’s surface pattern to determine strain as a function of temperature. For this purpose, the samples were coated with a white background and fine, well-distributed black speckles to create an appropriate contrast pattern. Two high-speed cameras recorded the strain evolution during heating. The ISTRA 4D software was used for system control, data acquisition, and analysis. The samples were heated from room temperature (RT) to 250 °C at a rate of 3 °C/min. Upon reaching the target temperature, a dwell time of 15 min was applied. To ensure reliable results, two complete heating - cooling cycles were performed, and the reported CTE values correspond to the second cycle. This approach compensates for potential stress effects that may influence measurements during the first cycle.

sections.heading: Fiber characterization
paragraphs: Prior to pressure infiltration, the fibers were characterized using SEM as shown in Fig.  1 . Measurements of the width, via image analysis using ImageJ [ 25 ], showed a mean of 9.91 μm with a deviation of 0.60 μm. The fiber surface is free of cracks but shows marginal roughness in the form of grooves along the fiber long axis forming as a likely result of the fiber production process [ 26 ]. Such grooves can potentially influence the matrix-fiber bonding characteristics but also the affinity to carbide formation due to an increased area of the melt-fiber interface. Therefore, this is of critical relevance to the subsequent properties of the MMC material.
Fig. 1 SEM images of the fibers prior to pressure infiltration in different magnifications. Slight surface grooves are visible in (c) marked with red arrows

sections.heading: Microstructures
paragraphs: The microstructures of the sample materials were analyzed by OLM and SEM. Figure  2  visualizes the micrographs, whereby (a) and (b) correspond to the unidirectional variants realized with different fiber contents (60 vol% and 70 vol%, respectively); (c) corresponds to the bidirectional variant, and (d) to the quasi-isotropic material. The microstructure of all materials clearly shows regions with higher and lower fiber densities. This is a result of the gas pressure infiltration technique as the fibers do not remain in the place of layup but are subject to displacement upon pressure infiltration. The void/defect content determined on the micrographs had a maximum of 1.03 vol%. However, most samples showed significantly lower fractions than this value.

The material variants with different layer orientations (c) and (d) clearly show the layered structures of the layups. It is noted that since the targets of the present work are the thermal conductivity properties, these alignment variations may affect the final properties only to a very limited extent since the thermal conduction is mainly caused along the fiber long axis.

Fig. 2 OLM images of the MMC materials with ( a ) and ( b ) unidirectional variants with different fiber contents; ( c ) bidirectional layup, ( d ) quasi-isotropic layup. Local variations and fiber densities as a result of pressure infiltration are visible as well as the layered structures in (c) and (d)

SEM micrographs taken in BSE mode of the UD1 sample are shown in Fig.  3 . The lower magnification shown in (a) visualizes similarly contrasted features as the OLM images. The higher magnification shown in (b) evidences the characteristics of individual fibers in the aluminum matrix. Slight surface roughness is evident, corresponding to the grooves clearly visible on the fiber surfaces in Fig.  1 (c). No cracks are evident in the interfacial regions suggesting proper bonding characteristics of matrix and fibers. A further important characteristic is the absence of pronounced carbide formation at the interfaces. These can form as a reaction product of liquid aluminum with the carbon fibers according to Al + C → Al 4 C 3  [ 27 ] and have detrimental effects on fiber-matrix bonding, crack formation, and propagation. Their formation can be suppressed to a large extent by (i) rapid cooling immediately after infiltration [ 23 ] and (ii) the choice of matrix alloy. The process used in the present work, gas pressure infiltration, is capable of realizing such high cooling rates counteracting the potential carbide formation. In addition, the alloying element Mg, which is present in the used aluminum matrix composition (see Sect.  2), has been shown to reduce the kinetics of carbide formation and was, therefore, used in the matrix alloy of the present study [ 28 ].

Fig. 3 SEM back-scattered electron images of the UD1 specimen with an overview in ( a ) and detailed features (fiber-cross-section reduction due to Al 4 C 3 -carbide-formation) in ( b ). Neither cracks nor interfacial carbides can be discriminated in these images

This relation indicates that time and temperature significantly contribute to the growth of the carbide layer. The resulting layer thickness can vary from a few nanometers for short exposure times at lower temperatures to several micrometers under prolonged exposure or in molten aluminum. Representative plots of the thickness calculated using Eq. ( 3 ) are shown in Fig.  4  as a function of temperature and time (Q = 200 kJ/mol, k₀ = 10⁻⁵ m²/s). Representative temperatures (600–660 °C) and dwell times (30–100 min) for SPS and VHP were extracted from Refs [ 16 ,  17 ,  20 ]. and are indicated with dashed lines in Fig.  4  (left). The estimated thickness ranges from 140 to 610 nm, which is in good agreement with observations of Al₄C₃ length of approximately 300–450 nm [ 17 ]. In contrast, the rapid infiltration and short dwell time of approximately 30 s at low temperature prevent excessive growth of the layer, resulting in a thickness roughly one order of magnitude lower.

Fig. 4 Representative plots using the parabolic growth law as a function of temperature and time (Q = 200 kJ/mol, k₀ = 10⁻⁵ m²/s) are shown; the black dashed line represents process conditions reported [ 16 ,  17 ,  20 ], while the red dashed line corresponds to the process conditions of the present study. A notably smaller layer thickness is predicted for the rapid infiltration process at low temperatures, characteristic of gas pressure infiltration

In aluminum MMCs with a high volume fraction of carbon fibers, the formation of Al₄C₃ at the fiber-matrix interface may be thermodynamically favored depending on the process conditions. The resulting reaction layer is extremely thin (Fig.  4 ), ranging from a few nanometers to the sub-micrometer range. An accurate identification of Al₄C₃ using conventional analytical techniques, e.g. SEM coupled with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), therefore remains challenging due to limitations in spatial resolution. The interaction volume of the electron beam extends by magnitudes the thickness of the Al₄C₃. Consequently, the measured signal is influenced by contributions from the surrounding aluminum matrix and carbon fibers. Furthermore, the detection of carbon using EDX is generally difficult due to the low energy of the C-K α  line and the limited sensitivity of the detectors to light elements. Additionally, spectral overlaps and contaminations further compromise reliability. In the present study, SEM coupled with EDX was attempted to detect and quantify the presence of Al₄C₃; however, due to the aforementioned limitations, a reliable quantitative analysis was not feasible – the limitation of this study is the absence of direct characterization of the interfaces. High-resolution techniques, such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and selective area electron diffraction (SAED), are more suitable, as they allow for direct determination of the dimensions and the crystal structure of Al₄C₃ on the nanometer or even atomic scale. This enables a direct resolution of the ultrathin interfacial reaction Al₄C₃ layer, however this is beyond the scope of this study.

sections.heading: Thermophysical property characterization
paragraphs: The thermophysical properties of the four MMC variants are summarized in Fig.  5  with their data tabulated in Appendix B. Both UD variants show extraordinarily high conduction values along the fiber long axis (x direction) with similar and low conduction values in y and z across directions. The results obtained here for the UD samples are close to the theoretical values using the fiber conductivity, λ f , matrix conductivity, λ M , and the fiber volume fractions, v f , which translate into ~ 526 W/mK for UD1 and ~ 595 W/mK for UD2 using the rule of mixture according to λ ≈ v f  × λ f  + (1- v f ) × λ M .

The obtained high values outperform earlier works, where short fibers were used and processed by a powder metallurgical route [ 17 ]. Zhu et al. [ 20 ] used an alternative approach, where long fibers were compressed with an aluminum powder matrix. While our results showcase conductivity values above the reported values along the fiber axis – a likely result of differing interface properties or potential effects of powder surface contamination – their values in across-directions closely match ours underpinning the validity of our results and measurement technique.

The bidirectional variant shows equivalent properties in x and y direction. Although this variant contains the same fiber fraction as the UD1 sample, the thermal conductivity is reduced by more than a factor of two. This non-linear behavior is a result of the low thermal conductivity properties of the fibers in the across-directions and the rule of mixture. The QI version contains three directions with very high conduction values, which are, however, not equivalent and interestingly higher than the bidirectional material. It is argued that through introduction of fibers in ± 45° orientations an interlinking of the conduction directions occurs. In case of the unidirectional or the bidirectional materials only fibers oriented along the x axis contribute to conduction in x direction. In contrast, in the QI material fibers along x as well as fibers in ± 45° proportionately contain conduction vectors along x providing additional thermal conductivity.

The statistical relevance of the results is demonstrated in Fig.  5  by the small standard deviation calculated from three individual measurements clearly showcasing the reproducibility of the reported results.
Fig. 5 Thermophysical property data of the different prepared MMC layups. ( a ) Thermal diffusivity, and ( b ) thermal conductivity

The coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) were determined for the four investigated material variants and are summarized in Fig.  6 . The variants UD1, UD2 and 0/90 (in both directions) show negative signs. The underlying reason for this is that pitch-based fibers generally show a low but negative CTE, whereas aluminum shows positive CTE values [ 32 ,  33 ]. Therefore, the MMCs behavior is dominated by the fiber’s properties, which is reasonable considering the high fraction of long fibers. The magnitude of CTE is likely caused by the fiber fraction as clearly visible for the UD variants. In case of the 0/90 variant, the directions contained a different number of layers explaining the high negative CTE in y direction as a result of the high fiber fraction in this direction. Finally, the QI variant shows a low but positive CTE. This can be explained by the complexity of the layup: The CTE of the layers with ± 45° fiber direction cancel out. Therefore, only a comparably low fiber volume content is available in 0° and 90°. Due the low fiber contents in these directions, the global material behavior is dominated by the matrix (positive) CTE.
Fig. 6 CTE for different directions of the MMC materials

sections.heading: Thermal shock
paragraphs: Typical exposure conditions encountered in space applications can involve rapid cooling and heating cycles. To simulate these conditions, a thermal shock experiment was conducted as described in Sect.  2 using the UD2 sample. After this treatment the sample was analyzed metallographically and thermally. A representative UD2 sample with the dimensions 143 × 65 × 2 mm (length × width × thickness) is presented. The other two samples of the same variant that were analyzed, exhibited similar behavior. Figure  7  shows an OLM overview image (a) and an SEM micrograph (b). The crack is difficult to observe and is, thus, highlighted by red arrows. While the majority of the sample remained intact, a few cracks are observed after the thermal shock treatment. The cracks predominantly propagate along the matrix/fiber interfaces through the thickness of the sample. At one location, three closely spaced cracks are visible and the longest section is 0.86 mm. This section is depicted in Fig.  7 . Due to the arrangement of fibers, the cracks can deviate as they are difficult to observe. The sections at different locations of the same sample showed similar behavior, however, the crack distribution is strongly linked to the random arrangement of the fibers.

To assess the effects of the thermal shock on the thermophysical properties, the thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity were determined equivalently to the untreated samples. For quantitative data see Table 1. The thermal conductivity properties decrease slightly likely as a result of the observed delaminations and cracks. Since the fibers themselves remain unfractured the majority of thermal conduction can still be provided through the fiber cross-sections.

Fig. 7 Micrographs of the UD2 sample after the thermal shock treatment. ( a ) OLM image; ( b ) SEM BSE image, where the crack is highlighted by red arrows  To summarize the determined thermophysical characteristics, property maps were collected and are visualized in Fig.  8 . All reference data used for this figure is listed in Table 2 in Appendix  C . Green visualizes the property fields determined in the present work. The other fields with different colors summarize and group literature data of different material categories. Among the many materials summarized here, the MMCs consisting of aluminum matrix and pitch-based fibers show among the lowest CTEs (neglecting the QI material for the moment), combined with very high thermal conductivities (see Fig.  8 (a)).

Considering the relation of thermal conductivity and density (Fig.  8 (b)), the material properties determined in the present work show an extraordinarily good balance of conductivity and density. The only materials with lower densities of relevance for thermal management applications are polymers and polymer-matrix composites (PMC), with, however, considerably lower thermal conduction and well-known degradation during thermal potential exposure to space radiation exposure. Additionally, long-term stability is an important aspect from the application perspective, which is oftentimes not given for polymeric materials that can be prone to environmental aging phenomena.
Fig. 8 Property maps for ( a ) thermal conductivity versus CTE and ( b ) thermal conductivity versus density

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: This study aimed at the development and characterization of light-weight materials with high thermal conductivity. For this purpose, an aluminum matrix was chosen together with carbon fibers. These aluminum MMC materials have been successfully processed by gas pressure infiltration technology. Pitch-based carbon fibers were used to tailor the thermal properties of the materials. Through the use of different layups it was possible to obtain different directionality behavior: UD1: ~ 400 W m − 1  K − 1 , UD2: ~ 530 W m − 1  K − 1 , 0/90: ~ 150 W m − 1  K − 1 , and QI: > 215 W m − 1  K − 1 . In addition, extremely low CTE values were determined, their sign being affected by the individual fiber layup.

The envisaged application of the investigated materials is in heat sinks for space applications. These structures frequently undergo thermal shocks through their exposure situations. Therefore, such a scenario was reproduced using repeated liquid nitrogen quenching. While minor cracks were found on metallographic specimens, only little reductions in thermal conductivities were observed suggesting that most of the fibers remained unaffected.

In summary, a promising material system was developed alongside adaptions of its processing technology. The obtained thermophysical properties are highly promising for their envisaged application. Further potential application scenarios remain to be explored.
